title: The Colonel's House to the Claustro de la Merced: Macondo, the Newsrooms, and the White Liqui-Liqui
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Aracataca, born in the house of Colonel Márquez
stops.date_confidence: attested; 6 March 1927 is the accepted date, though a 1928 counter-claim circulates in family testimony and in Gerald Martin's biography and is unconfirmed here. The coordinate is the birth house at Carrera 5 #6-35, now the Casa Museo, per Nominatim and Spanish Wikipedia, and corrects a value some 250 metres southwest of it.
stops.campa: Gabriel José García Márquez is born in his maternal grandparents' house in Aracataca, a banana town of the Magdalena going quietly broke. His father Gabriel Eligio García is a telegraph operator the family did not want; his mother Luisa Santiaga Márquez Iguarán married him against her parents' wishes and was forgiven only slowly. The infant is left behind with the grandparents when the couple move on. The house has a room kept for the saints, a yard with an almond tree, and a colonel who fought the Thousand Days' War on the Liberal side and lost it.
stops.quote: The air was so damp that fish could have come in through the doors and swum out the windows.
stops.quote_source: One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), trans. Gregory Rabassa (English ed. 1970)
suggested_refs: The Casa Museo Gabriel García Márquez at Carrera 5 #6-35, Aracataca, reconstructed in 2010 from descriptions in Vivir para contarla

stops.name: Ciénaga, the massacre at the railway station
stops.date_confidence: attested for the massacre on the night of 5 to 6 December 1928, with the death toll disputed between roughly forty-seven and two thousand. García Márquez was twenty-one months old and living in the same region: he was not a witness, and this stop marks family memory, not presence. A source giving the massacre as happening before his birth is wrong by twenty-one months and is corrected here.
stops.campa: Soldiers fire on United Fruit Company strikers gathered by the railway station at Ciénaga, an hour up the line from Aracataca. The government denies that the killings took place. The count of the dead is argued over for the rest of the century and never settled. The toddler in the colonel's house hears the story afterwards, from the colonel, in the form it will keep: bodies loaded onto a train, the train running to the sea, and the official record insisting nothing happened. Forty years later he writes it with three thousand dead and one survivor nobody believes.
suggested_refs: The Prometeo de la Libertad monument of 1978 on the station plaza at Ciénaga, raised to the banana workers

stops.name: Aracataca, the colonel and the grandmother
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the grandparental upbringing runs from 1927 to 1936 and the year given here orders the segment rather than dating a single event. The Montessori enrolment is placed at 1933 by the Instituto Cervantes chronology.
stops.campa: The boy grows up between two ways of speaking. Colonel Nicolás Márquez takes him to the circus and to see ice, and tells him about the war, the amnesties, and the veteran's pension that never arrives. Tranquilina Iguarán runs a household where the dead come back at fixed hours and where a ghost is reported in the same voice used for the price of flour. He learns that the way to have an impossible thing believed is to say it without raising the voice. At the Montessori school in the town he learns to read before he can do arithmetic.
stops.quote: It always amuses me that the biggest praise for my work comes for the imagination, while the truth is that there's not a single line in all my work that does not have a basis in reality.
stops.quote_source: The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 69,' interview with Peter H. Stone, Issue 82, Winter 1981
suggested_refs: The floorplan of the Aracataca house, hand-drawn by García Márquez in 1978, Harry Ransom Center

stops.name: Sincé, the family without the colonel
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1936 move, which the Instituto Cervantes chronology gives as Sincé in Sucre, not Sincelejo some thirty kilometres away; the file corrects the town and the coordinate. The colonel's death follows in March 1937 at Aracataca. Banrepcultural records a later move to the river port of Sucre, staged separately.
stops.campa: The family moves to Sincé in the department of Sucre, and the grandfather stays behind in Aracataca. In March of the following year the colonel dies at seventy-three, and the house with the almond tree and the room for the saints stops being a place the boy can return to. He is nine years old. From here he lives with parents he hardly knows, in towns that belong to his father's work rather than to him. His mother is running a household of small children on a telegraphist's income, and he is one more of them.
suggested_refs: The Instituto Cervantes chronology for 1936-1937, which fixes the move and the colonel's death

stops.name: Barranquilla, boarder at the Colegio San José
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1940 by the Instituto Cervantes chronology.
stops.campa: He enters the Jesuit Colegio San José in Barranquilla as a boarder, thirteen years old, and meets a city for the first time: river port, customs house, Syrian and Italian shopkeepers, a Caribbean commerce that runs on rumour. He writes verses for the school magazine and is noticed for them. The Jesuits keep the day on a bell and the boys in a dormitory. What he takes from the four years is the walk down to the river, the cranes standing over the wharf, and the smell coming off the customs sheds at two in the afternoon.
suggested_refs: The school magazine of the Colegio San José, Barranquilla, carrier of his earliest published verses

stops.name: Zipaquirá, the scholarship in the cold
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1943 to 1946 span at the Liceo Nacional. Banrepcultural states that he took the bachillerato in 1946, which the file follows against a source giving 1947; a February 1947 matriculation at the Universidad Nacional requires the earlier date. The claim that he excelled at sports and captained a team is unsupported by any source reached and is not repeated.
stops.campa: On a state scholarship he boards at the Liceo Nacional de Varones in Zipaquirá, a salt-mining town on the Andean plateau where the fog comes down in the afternoon and the boys wear wool. A Caribbean boy is sent up to the interior to be improved. He reads whatever the school library holds, writes poems in the manner of whoever he read last, and is remembered by classmates as thin, formal, and permanently cold. He takes the bachillerato in December 1946.
suggested_refs: The Liceo Nacional de Varones at Zipaquirá and its surviving school publications of 1943-1946

stops.name: Sucre, the girl at the river port
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the Instituto Cervantes chronology dates the meeting with Mercedes Barcha to 1943, on a school holiday in Sucre, where the family had settled. The month is set to order the segment. The 1951 killing referred to in the campa occurs later, in the same town, and is attested through the family's own account.
stops.campa: Home from the plateau for the holidays, in the river port of Sucre where his parents now live, he sees Mercedes Raquel Barcha Pardo, a pharmacist's daughter, thirteen years old. He tells people he is going to marry her. He does, fifteen years later. The town holds something else for him too. In 1951 two brothers here kill a man for their sister's honour in front of everyone, having announced what they mean to do to every person they meet, and thirty years afterwards he writes the killing down close to the way it stood. Why nobody in the town stopped it is the question the book keeps putting and never answers.
stops.quote: Santiago Nasar had often told me that the smell of closed-in flowers had an immediate relation to death for him.
stops.quote_source: Chronicle of a Death Foretold (1981), trans. Gregory Rabassa, p. 47
suggested_refs: Crónica de una muerte anunciada (1981), the novelized reconstruction of the 1951 Sucre killing

segments.name: The Fire in Bogotá and the Newsrooms of the Coast

stops.name: Bogotá, law at the Universidad Nacional and a first story
stops.date_confidence: attested; matriculation in law in February 1947 per the Instituto Cervantes chronology, and the publication of La tercera resignación in El Espectador on 13 September 1947.
stops.campa: He matriculates in law at the Universidad Nacional because the family wants a doctor of laws and because a scholarship covers it. He attends as little as he can manage. In a boarding house near the centre he reads Kafka's Metamorphosis and understands that a story may announce the impossible in its first sentence and then simply proceed. On 13 September El Espectador prints La tercera resignación, his first published story, with a note from Eduardo Zalamea Borda welcoming a writer nobody has heard of. He is twenty, and still enrolled in law.
suggested_refs: El Espectador, 13 September 1947, first printing of La tercera resignación with Zalamea Borda's introductory note

stops.name: Bogotá, the ninth of April
stops.date_confidence: attested for the assassination of Jorge Eliécer Gaitán at Carrera 7 and Avenida Jiménez; the chronology places García Márquez nearby rather than at the corner, and the coordinate marks the shooting.
stops.campa: Jorge Eliécer Gaitán is shot on the Carrera Séptima a few blocks from the boarding house. By nightfall the centre of Bogotá is burning: trams overturned, shopfronts opened, a crowd hunting the killer and then hunting whatever else it finds. The university closes indefinitely. The boarding house burns with his papers inside it, the unfinished stories among them. La Violencia begins here and runs a decade through the countryside he came from. He leaves for the coast.
suggested_refs: The Bogotazo of 9 April 1948 and the destruction of the colonial cloister on Calle 11, later the site of the Centro Cultural Gabriel García Márquez

stops.name: Cartagena, law nominally, El Universal actually
stops.date_confidence: attested for the transfer to the Universidad de Cartagena and the work at El Universal in 1948. The exact street address of the 1948 newsroom is unconfirmed and the coordinate marks the old walled town where the paper operated; the month is set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He transfers his law registration to the Universidad de Cartagena inside the walls and takes work at El Universal, where the editor Clemente Manuel Zabala goes through his sentences with a pencil and strikes out the adjectives. Censorship is in force and the paper writes around it. He learns the difference between a fact and a phrase about a fact. He files short pieces at night for very little money, and stops pretending about the law degree, which he never finishes.
stops.quote: I began my career as a journalist in Colombia and working as a reporter is something I never stopped being.
stops.quote_source: Interview with Gabriel García Márquez, Columbia University School of International and Public Affairs, 1983 transcript
suggested_refs: The columns of El Universal, Cartagena, 1948-1949, edited by Clemente Manuel Zabala
sources: CVC Instituto Cervantes, 'Cartagena de Indias: personalidades, García Márquez'

stops.name: Barranquilla, La Jirafa and the group
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1950 to 1952 period at El Heraldo. La Cueva, the bar usually attached to the Barranquilla Group in later accounts, opened only in 1954, after he had left the city; in these years the circle met at the Café Colombia, the Café Roma and around Ramón Vinyes's bookshop, and the coordinate marks that district.
stops.campa: He writes La Jirafa for El Heraldo, a daily column signed at times Septimus, for money that does not cover a room. He sleeps in a building whose other tenants are prostitutes and pays the watchman in manuscript pages when he has no coins. Around the Catalan bookseller Ramón Vinyes he falls in with Álvaro Cepeda Samudio, Germán Vargas and Alfonso Fuenmayor, who put Faulkner and Woolf into his hands and argue with him past dawn about an invented county in Mississippi and what a novelist is allowed to build out of one town. He is twenty-three.
suggested_refs: The La Jirafa columns of El Heraldo, Barranquilla, 1950-1952, collected as Textos costeños

stops.name: Aracataca, the town gone small
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1952 by the Instituto Cervantes chronology; the month is not fixed and is set to order the segment.
stops.campa: He returns with his mother to sell the grandparents' house. The train crosses the banana zone past plantations gone back to dust; the town has shrunk, the streets are shorter than he remembers, the heat stands still at two in the afternoon. In the pharmacy his mother greets a woman she has not seen in years, says her name aloud, and the two of them sit down and cry. He is twenty-four. He goes back to Barranquilla with the beginning of a novel about a corpse waiting to be buried, and with the name Macondo, read off a plantation sign on the line.
suggested_refs: La hojarasca (1955), the first appearance of Macondo in print

stops.name: Bogotá, staff reporter at El Espectador
stops.date_confidence: attested; Banrepcultural dates the return to Bogotá as staff reporter to February 1954. A source that puts the shipwreck series in this same month is wrong: that is an April 1955 event, staged separately here.
stops.campa: He comes back to the capital as staff reporter and film critic for El Espectador and is paid, for the first time, enough to eat every day. He reviews the films that reach Bogotá, covers a landslide in Antioquia, and files reportage written like fiction and checked like reporting. In 1955 La hojarasca appears, a short first novel in which a colonel, his daughter and his grandson sit through an afternoon with an unburied doctor in a town called Macondo. The reviews are respectful. It sells almost nothing.
suggested_refs: The film criticism and reportage of El Espectador, 1954-1955, collected as Entre cachacos

stops.name: Bogotá, fourteen days of the shipwrecked sailor
stops.date_confidence: attested; the destroyer ARC Caldas lost eight men on 28 February 1955 and the fourteen-part series ran in April 1955 per the English Wikipedia entry on The Story of a Shipwrecked Sailor.
stops.campa: Luis Alejandro Velasco, a sailor who spent ten days on a raft in the Caribbean and came ashore a decorated hero of the navy, sits with him through twenty sessions. What he describes is a destroyer carrying contraband cargo lashed on deck, the cargo shifting, and eight men going into the water in calm weather. It was the Rojas Pinilla government that pinned the medal on him. El Espectador runs the account in fourteen instalments under Velasco's own byline, circulation doubles, and the government closes the paper the following year.
suggested_refs: Relato de un náufrago, the 1955 El Espectador series reissued in book form in 1970
sources: Wikipedia, 'The Story of a Shipwrecked Sailor' (English)

segments.name: Europe, and the Newspaper That Was Closed

stops.name: Geneva, the summit at the Palais des Nations
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1955 by the Instituto Cervantes chronology; the Four Power conference sat from 18 to 23 July and the day of his arrival is not fixed.
stops.campa: El Espectador sends him to Europe as a correspondent, partly because a story is expected of him and partly because his reporting has become inconvenient at home. He covers the summit at the Palais des Nations, where the four powers sit for a week and settle very little, and files copy on the tailoring of the delegates and on the way important men behave when a camera is pointed at them. It is his first crossing of the Atlantic. The conference sits from the eighteenth of July to the twenty-third and ends in a communiqué that commits nobody to anything.
suggested_refs: The 1955 European dispatches of El Espectador, collected as De Europa y América

stops.name: Rome, the film school on the Via Tuscolana
stops.date_confidence: attested that he studied at the Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia in 1955 without taking a qualification, per the Harry Ransom Center exhibition pages. The coordinate is the school's own site beside Cinecittà per Italian Wikipedia and corrects a widely copied value some thirteen kilometres away in northern Rome. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He enrolls at the Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia beside the Cinecittà lots, in the years when Italian directors are filming ordinary people in the street with the camera at eye level. He learns to break a story into shots and to cut. He takes no qualification. Cinema stays with him afterwards as a half-finished second trade: screenplays for hire, adaptations of his own books that he dislikes, and thirty years later a film school of his own outside Havana. He never sells the film rights to Cien años de soledad in his lifetime.
suggested_refs: The Centro Sperimentale di Cinematografia, Via Tuscolana 1520, Rome

stops.name: Paris, rue Cujas, the paper closed behind him
stops.date_confidence: attested that he lived in the Latin Quarter through 1956 and 1957 without paying rent after the Rojas Pinilla dictatorship shut El Espectador; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: The dictatorship shuts El Espectador and his salary stops arriving in a city where he knows nobody. He lives in a hotel on the rue Cujas on unpaid credit, returns bottles for coins, and reads the newspapers left on café tables because he cannot buy one. In that room he writes El coronel no tiene quien le escriba, about an old man who walks to the post office every Friday for a pension letter that does not come, and rewrites it nine times. The hotel keeper carries the bill for more than a year.
suggested_refs: El coronel no tiene quien le escriba, serialized in Revista Mito in 1958 and published in book form by Aguirre Editor, Medellín, in 1961

stops.name: Caracas, Momento, and a dictator falling
stops.date_confidence: attested; he reached Caracas at the end of 1957 by way of Eastern Europe and London and was present for the fall of Marcos Pérez Jiménez on 23 January 1958.
stops.campa: He arrives in Caracas with a suitcase of unpublished manuscripts and takes a job at the magazine Momento. Weeks later the regime of Marcos Pérez Jiménez collapses. He is in the presidential palace in the hours afterwards and watches an officer back out of a room with a pistol still in his hand while a whole country waits in the street outside. The scene stays with him for eighteen years, until he writes a book about a tyrant so old that nobody alive can remember his beginning.
stops.quote: A lie is more comfortable than doubt, more useful than love, more lasting than truth.
stops.quote_source: The Autumn of the Patriarch (1976), trans. Gregory Rabassa, p. 254
suggested_refs: El otoño del patriarca (1975), whose composition García Márquez traced to the fall of Pérez Jiménez

stops.name: Barranquilla, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested to 21 March 1958 at Barranquilla per the English Wikipedia entry on Mercedes Barcha. Spanish Wikipedia names the Iglesia de Nuestra Señora del Perpetuo Socorro; the Instituto Cervantes chronology names no parish, and the church could not be fixed to street precision, so the coordinate falls back to the central city rather than assert an address.
stops.campa: He flies back from Caracas and marries Mercedes Barcha, fifteen years after telling a river port that he would. She is twenty-five and has waited through Bogotá, Cartagena, Paris and Caracas with very little correspondence to go on, and her father, a pharmacist, has been told for years that this was coming. They fly back to Venezuela together the same week and he is at the magazine again within days. She runs the household and the money for the next fifty-six years, and it is she who decides which of those years he can afford to spend earning nothing.
suggested_refs: The Iglesia de Nuestra Señora del Perpetuo Socorro, Barrio Boston, Barranquilla, named as the parish in Spanish-language accounts

segments.name: Prensa Latina, and the Road to Mexico

stops.name: Bogotá, the birth of Rodrigo
stops.date_confidence: attested to 24 August 1959 at Bogotá by the Instituto Cervantes chronology, Spanish Wikipedia and Banrepcultural, correcting a widely repeated 1958 Caracas date and a hedge that the birthplace was 'reported variably' between Colombia and Mexico. Mexico is impossible: the family did not move there until 1961. The Camilo Torres baptism is reported but not confirmed in this pass.
stops.campa: Their first son Rodrigo is born in Bogotá on the twenty-fourth of August, where the couple have come to open the Colombian office of Prensa Latina, the news agency set up in Havana in the first year of the revolution. The father is thirty-two and has published two short books that sold nothing at all; the household lives on an agency salary paid from Cuba. The family friend said to have baptised the child is Camilo Torres, a priest who will leave the church for the guerrilla and be killed carrying a rifle in 1966.
suggested_refs: The Instituto Cervantes chronology under 1959, 'Nace el día 24 de agosto su primer hijo, Rodrigo'

stops.name: Havana, the agency in the first year
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1959 to 1960; he was invited to Havana for Operación Verdad in January 1959 and worked much of 1960 for Prensa Latina under Jorge Ricardo Masetti.
stops.campa: Invited to Havana to watch the revolution try its enemies in public, he stays to work for Prensa Latina under the Argentine Jorge Ricardo Masetti, an agency built to break the wire monopoly of the North American services. The newsroom runs on coffee and improvisation. He edits copy out of every country in the hemisphere and takes on, in the same year, a political allegiance and a set of friends inside a government, which is a different thing from an opinion and much harder to put down. Some nights he sleeps on the office floor.
suggested_refs: Prensa Latina under Jorge Ricardo Masetti, 1959-1961

stops.name: New York, the bureau under threat
stops.date_confidence: attested for early 1961. His FBI file, released under FOIA and reported by the Washington Post in 2015, documents surveillance of this period; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Posted to the Prensa Latina bureau near Rockefeller Center, he works with an iron bar beside the telephone and answers calls from anti-Castro exiles who promise to come up the stairs. Mercedes and the baby are in the apartment. The Bay of Pigs landing fails in April. Pro-Soviet cadres take the agency out of Masetti's hands and he resigns with Masetti's circle; the break is with the agency and not with Havana, where he keeps going back for the next thirty years. He is thirty-three, out of a job, and in a country whose federal police have opened a file on him.
stops.quote: It bothers me that the people of the United States have appropriated the word America as if they were the only Americans.
stops.quote_source: Interview with Gabriel García Márquez, Columbia University School of International and Public Affairs, 1983 transcript
suggested_refs: The FBI file on García Márquez, released under FOIA and reported by the Washington Post, 3 September 2015
sources: Washington Post, 'Love in the time of surveillance,' 3 September 2015

stops.name: Alabama, the Greyhound through the segregated South
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the family's bus journey from New York to Mexico in 1961 is reported in family accounts and in Gerald Martin's biography, but the route and its halts are not documented. The coordinate marks the Deep South corridor generally and not a known stop.
stops.campa: Without money for the flight he takes Mercedes and the two-year-old across the United States by Greyhound, twelve days, in the summer that Freedom Riders are being beaten in these same bus stations. Hotels turn the family away for looking Mexican. Out of the window is the country Faulkner wrote, the courthouse squares and the pine and the standing heat and the doors marked white only, and he has been reading it since Barranquilla. The route and the halts are recorded nowhere. What survives of the crossing is the twelve days and the refusals at the desks.
suggested_refs: Gerald Martin, Gabriel García Márquez: A Life (2008), on the 1961 bus journey
sources: Gerald Martin biography as cited in secondary press coverage

stops.name: Mexico City, San Ángel
stops.date_confidence: attested that the family reached Mexico City in mid-1961 and settled there permanently; the exact day of arrival is not fixed here.
stops.campa: They arrive in Mexico City with a hundred dollars and stay for the rest of his life. He edits two women's magazines, writes advertising copy, and takes screenplay work, including an adaptation of Juan Rulfo's El gallo de oro made with Carlos Fuentes. For four years he publishes almost no fiction of his own, and the friends he makes in Mexico take him for a journalist who once wrote a novel. Rulfo's Pedro Páramo he reads twice through in a single night, and afterwards he can recite pages of it.
suggested_refs: El gallo de oro (1964), screenplay by García Márquez and Carlos Fuentes from Juan Rulfo

stops.name: Mexico City, the birth of Gonzalo and a book he disowns
stops.date_confidence: attested to 16 April 1962 for Gonzalo's birth per the Instituto Cervantes chronology. La mala hora appeared in Madrid in 1962, not 1961: a source collapsing it with the 1961 Medellín edition of El coronel no tiene quien le escriba is corrected here against Spanish Wikipedia.
stops.campa: Their second son Gonzalo is born in Mexico City. In the same year a Madrid house prints La mala hora and its editors quietly correct the book into peninsular Spanish, replacing his coastal words with the words used in Castile. He repudiates the edition and has the novel published again in Mexico, four years later, in the words he used. It is the last book he publishes for five years. The intervening work is advertising copy and screenplays, for employers who mostly do not know he is a novelist at all.
suggested_refs: The repudiated Madrid first edition of La mala hora, 1962, and the corrected Mexican edition of 1966

stops.name: The Acapulco road, the car turned around
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the turn-back is García Márquez's own account, retold with changing comic detail over decades, and the Ransom Center's scholarship flags it as partly mythologised. The point on the highway is not documented and is approximated.
stops.campa: Driving the family to Acapulco for a holiday, somewhere on the road out of Mexico City the whole book arrives at once: the voice, the tone, the first sentence, the colonel in front of the firing squad remembering the afternoon his father took him to discover ice. He has been circling this material for seventeen years and could never find the register for it. He stops the car on the highway and turns it around. Mercedes asks how long this is going to take. Eighteen months, he tells her, which turns out to be close. The story is his own, and he told it differently every time he was asked.
suggested_refs: Álvaro Santana-Acuña, Ascent to Glory (2020), on the accretion of the origin story
sources: Harry Ransom Center Magazine, 'Ascent to Glory,' 30 May 2020

stops.name: Mexico City, the room behind the house
stops.date_confidence: attested for the roughly eighteen months of composition through 1965 and 1966 in Mexico City. The street is cited widely in the biographical literature, Gerald Martin above all, and the coordinate is approximate; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He works every day from nine until three in a small room behind the house, smoking through the morning, with a rose on the desk that Mercedes keeps replacing. Outside the room the debts run: the car sold, then the television, the radio, the refrigerator, the jewellery, then credit at the butcher and nine months of rent carried by a landlord who never asks. He hands her the pages. She reads none of them until it is finished. When he stops he owes about ten thousand dollars.
stops.quote: On a good working day, working from nine o'clock in the morning to two or three in the afternoon, the most I can write is a short paragraph of four or five lines.
stops.quote_source: The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 69,' Issue 82, Winter 1981
suggested_refs: Gerald Martin, Gabriel García Márquez: A Life (2008), on the composition of Cien años de soledad
sources: Harry Ransom Center Magazine, 'Ascent to Glory,' 30 May 2020

stops.name: Mexico City, the typescript posted in halves
stops.date_confidence: attested that they could not pay the full postage on the typescript to Editorial Sudamericana. The much-repeated detail that they sent the wrong half first accreted years after publication, per Álvaro Santana-Acuña's archival work, and is not asserted here. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: The typescript runs to some thirteen hundred pages. At the counter the clerk weighs the parcel and names a price they do not have, so they send as much as the coins will carry and pawn what is left at home to send the rest. The heater and the hair dryer go to the pawnshop in the same week. The parcel travels to Buenos Aires. Whether the halves went in the right order is a detail that entered the story long afterwards, and neither of them ever settled it.
suggested_refs: Álvaro Santana-Acuña's archival reconstruction of the manuscript's dispatch, Ascent to Glory (2020)
sources: Harry Ransom Center Magazine, 'Ascent to Glory,' 30 May 2020

stops.name: Buenos Aires, eight thousand copies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the end of May 1967 for the first Editorial Sudamericana edition. The coordinate is the publisher's address at Humberto Primo 555 per Spanish Wikipedia and corrects a value some 2.5 kilometres north in Retiro. The exact day of release is given variously within May and June.
stops.campa: Editorial Sudamericana prints Cien años de soledad in an edition of about eight thousand copies and expects to sell them across a year. They go in a fortnight. He is forty, and in May he could not pay his rent. The book is reprinted and reprinted; three years later Gregory Rabassa's English version carries it out of the language, and its author says afterwards that he prefers the translation to his own text. It has since reached forty-six languages and more than fifty million copies.
stops.quote: Caribbean reality resembles the wildest imagination.
stops.quote_source: The Paris Review, 'The Art of Fiction No. 69,' Issue 82, Winter 1981
suggested_refs: The first Editorial Sudamericana edition of Cien años de soledad, Buenos Aires, 1967; Gregory Rabassa's One Hundred Years of Solitude, 1970

stops.name: Barcelona, Sarrià, and the patriarch
stops.date_confidence: attested; the family moved to Barcelona in the autumn of 1967 and remained until 1975. The 1972 Rómulo Gallegos Prize was awarded for Cien años de soledad and not, as one compilation has it, for the Eréndira collection published the same year; the donation of the money to the Movimiento al Socialismo is reported in biographical accounts and not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: The family moves to Barcelona in the last years of Franco, into the circle around the agent Carmen Balcells, who has begun treating Latin American novelists as an economic force rather than a literary movement. Here he writes El otoño del patriarca, enormous circling sentences about a dictator so old that his death has to be verified twice, built out of Pérez Jiménez and Gómez and Trujillo and out of the old man ruling the country he is living in. In 1972 Venezuela gives him the Rómulo Gallegos Prize for Cien años de soledad. The money is reported to have gone to the Movimiento al Socialismo, though no account of the transfer has been traced.
suggested_refs: The Carmen Balcells agency papers on the Boom contracts of 1967-1975

stops.name: Barcelona, the eleventh of September
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the coup is attested, and the pledge to publish no fiction until Chile was free is widely reported in the biographical literature, but no primary text of the pledge was reached in this pass. Neither salvador_allende.journey.json nor augusto_pinochet.journey.json currently names him.
stops.campa: The Chilean air force bombs La Moneda, Salvador Allende dies inside it, and Augusto Pinochet takes the country. From Barcelona he announces that he will publish no more fiction while the dictatorship stands, and for several years he does not, giving the time to reporting and to founding a political magazine instead. Pinochet holds power for seventeen years. The silence breaks first, in 1981, with a short novel about a murder in a Colombian river town. No primary text of the pledge has been traced; it reaches us through the reporting of other people.
suggested_refs: The magazine Alternativa, Bogotá, founded 1974, product of the political-journalism years

stops.name: Rome, the Russell Tribunal
stops.date_confidence: attested through Julio Cortázar's own journey file, which seats García Márquez beside him with Armando Uribe at the opening Rome session of the second Russell Tribunal in 1974. The day within the session is not fixed and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: He sits with Julio Cortázar and Armando Uribe at the opening session of the second Russell Tribunal, convened in Rome to hear evidence on the dictatorships of Latin America: the disappeared of Chile, of Brazil, of Uruguay, read into a record no state has agreed to honour. The Colombian and the Argentine have already divided once, over Cuba. Cortázar signed the international protest of 1971 over Heberto Padilla's forced self-criticism and García Márquez did not. They are at the same table anyway.
suggested_refs: The proceedings of the second Russell Tribunal, Rome session, 1974

stops.name: Mexico City, the punch at the Palacio de Bellas Artes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the blow at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in 1976 per the English Wikipedia entry on Mario Vargas Llosa, correcting a compilation that placed it at an unidentified cinema three kilometres away. The day, 12 February, comes from contemporaneous reporting. A motive is reported at second hand through a mutual friend; neither man ever gave an account of his own.
stops.campa: At a film event Mario Vargas Llosa walks up to him and knocks him to the floor with one blow to the face. The two men had been friends since 1967, had held a public dialogue in Lima on the Latin American novel, had lived streets apart in Barcelona, and one of them had written a doctoral thesis about the other. Neither ever gives a public account of the motive; what circulates comes at second hand, through a mutual friend. Two days later Rodrigo Moya photographs the black eye, and puts the negative in a drawer for thirty years.
suggested_refs: Rodrigo Moya's 1976 photographs of the black eye, released in 2007
La novela en América Latina: diálogo (1968), the Lima conversation of 1967
sources: The Paris Review blog, 'When Mario Vargas Llosa Punched Gabriel García Márquez,' 6 March 2019

stops.name: Stockholm, the announcement at the Börshuset
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Swedish Academy announced the prize on 21 October 1982. The coordinate is the Stock Exchange Building on Stortorget in Gamla Stan, which houses the Academy, and corrects a value about 150 metres east.
stops.campa: The Swedish Academy announces the Nobel Prize in Literature for his novels and short stories, in which the fantastic and the realistic are combined in a richly composed world of imagination, reflecting a continent's life and conflicts. He is fifty-five, and the first Colombian given the prize. At home the news is handled as a national event rather than a literary one: the government offers him an aircraft, and the newspapers clear their front pages for the better part of a week.
suggested_refs: The Swedish Academy citation of 21 October 1982
sources: Nobel Foundation, prize facts for Literature 1982

stops.name: Stockholm, the white liqui-liqui
stops.date_confidence: attested for the ceremony at the Konserthuset on 10 December 1982; the lecture was delivered on 8 December. The coordinate is Hötorget 8 per English Wikipedia and corrects a value about 200 metres northeast.
stops.campa: He takes the medal in a white liqui-liqui, the Caribbean linen suit buttoned to the collar, among five hundred men in white tie, and brings sixty Colombian musicians and dancers with him to Stockholm. Two days earlier he read La soledad de América Latina to the Academy. The lecture sets the chroniclers' fabulous inventories of the New World against the arithmetic of the continent's dead, and asks the Europeans who find the novels implausible to hold the history to the same measure.
stops.quote: A new and sweeping utopia of life, where no one will be able to decide for others how they die, where love will prove true and happiness be possible, and where the races condemned to one hundred years of solitude will have, at last and forever, a second opportunity on earth.
stops.quote_source: Nobel Lecture, 'The Solitude of Latin America,' Stockholm, 8 December 1982, closing paragraph, official English translation
suggested_refs: La soledad de América Latina, Nobel Lecture, 8 December 1982
sources: Nobel Foundation, Nobel Lecture 1982 (fetched via proxy render after a direct 403)

stops.name: San Antonio de los Baños, the film school on the sugar plain
stops.date_confidence: attested; the Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión was created in 1985 and inaugurated on 15 December 1986, with Fernando Birri and Julio García Espinosa. The coordinate corrects a value about five kilometres southeast. The Cubanacán protocol house and the domestic scenes of the Castro friendship rest on García Márquez's own account to Pete Hamill in Vanity Fair, which could not be refetched in this pass and is carried as reported.
stops.campa: With Fernando Birri and Julio García Espinosa he founds a film school for Latin America on a former plantation outside Havana: students housed and taught for nothing, by whichever directors will come and teach. Fidel Castro backs it. In these years the Cuban government keeps a protocol house for him at Cubanacán, where Castro cooks in the kitchen, brings books to argue about, and takes him fishing. He also spends the friendship: prisoners leave the island on lists he carries in person and does not publicise.
suggested_refs: The Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión, San Antonio de los Baños, and the Fundación del Nuevo Cine Latinoamericano
sources: Wikipedia (Spanish), 'Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión'
Vanity Fair, March 1988, Pete Hamill on García Márquez and Castro (inaccessible on refetch, cited per dossier)

stops.name: Cartagena, the Liberator on the river
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1989 publication of El general en su laberinto. The coordinate is Cartagena, at the Caribbean end of the Magdalena route the novel retraces, rather than a single writing address; the month orders the segment.
stops.campa: He publishes El general en su laberinto, which puts Simón Bolívar on a barge going down the Magdalena in 1830, dying, forty-six years old, swearing, driven out by the republics he made. He had the river charted and the Liberator's last months reconstructed day by day before writing a line of it. Bolivarian historians and serving army officers object that the founder of five countries is shown incontinent, foul-mouthed and abandoned. He answers that the documents say so.
suggested_refs: El general en su laberinto (1989) and the day-by-day itinerary of Bolívar's 1830 descent of the Magdalena compiled for it

stops.name: Cartagena, a school for reporters
stops.date_confidence: attested for the mid-1990s founding of the Fundación para un Nuevo Periodismo Iberoamericano, now the Fundación Gabo. Sources give both 1994 and 1995 for the founding year and this file does not adjudicate between them.
stops.campa: He puts his own money and his own name into a foundation in Cartagena that runs workshops for working Latin American reporters, taught by reporters, with no diplomas and no theory. He teaches in them himself, going through drafts line by line the way Clemente Manuel Zabala went through his at El Universal half a century earlier, a few streets from where the workshops now sit. Sessions run a week at a time, a small group to a room, and he sits at the table with them and takes the drafts one by one.
stops.quote: I do every kind of journalism—except interviews.
stops.quote_source: Interview with Gabriel García Márquez, Columbia University School of International and Public Affairs, 1983 transcript
suggested_refs: The Fundación para un Nuevo Periodismo Iberoamericano, Cartagena, now the Fundación Gabo

stops.name: Bogotá, the kidnappings written down
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1996 publication of Noticia de un secuestro, reconstructing the 1990 and 1991 abductions carried out by Los Extraditables on Pablo Escobar's orders. A 2015 allegation by a former Escobar lieutenant concerning letters to Havana is unverified and is not repeated. The month orders the segment; pablo_escobar.journey.json carries no stop naming García Márquez.
stops.campa: He spends three years on Noticia de un secuestro, a book with no invention in it: ten Colombians taken hostage across 1990 and 1991 by the men working for Pablo Escobar, to force a government to give up extradition to the United States. He interviews the hostages who came home and the families of the two who did not. The method is the one he used on Velasco forty years earlier, sitting with the survivor and taking the account down until it holds together. He is sixty-nine.
suggested_refs: Noticia de un secuestro (1996) and the testimony of the surviving hostages of Los Extraditables

stops.name: Mexico City, the late books
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 2002 publication of Vivir para contarla and the October 2004 novella. The 1999 lymphatic cancer treated in Los Angeles is attested, but the treating hospital is not established: English Wikipedia says only a hospital in Los Angeles, coverage of the time most often names UCLA, and a compilation naming Cedars-Sinai is a guess, so no separate stop is made for it. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: Treated for lymphatic cancer in Los Angeles in 1999, he works faster afterwards. Vivir para contarla covers the childhood, the newsroom years and the coast, and stops before the fame; two further volumes are announced and never arrive. In 2004 pirated copies of Memoria de mis putas tristes appear in the Colombian streets before the authorised printing, so he rewrites the final chapter and the bootleg becomes the wrong book. He is seventy-seven. No further fiction appears in his lifetime.
stops.quote: Life is not what one lived, but what one remembers and how one remembers it in order to recount it.
stops.quote_source: Living to Tell the Tale (2002), trans. Edith Grossman (2004), epigraph
suggested_refs: Vivir para contarla (2002), the only completed volume of a projected three-part memoir
sources: Wikiquote sourced entry for the Grossman epigraph
Penguin Random House reading guide, Living to Tell the Tale

stops.name: Mexico City, the house at Pedregal de San Ángel
stops.date_confidence: attested; his brother Jaime disclosed the dementia publicly in 2012, and the death is dated 17 April 2014 at Mexico City, aged eighty-seven. The immediate cause reported by El País is a heart attack against a background of infection, prior lymphoma and dementia; the El País page was blocked on direct refetch and is carried per the dossier's account of the coverage.
stops.campa: In 2012 his brother Jaime says publicly what the household has been managing in private: the memory is going, he can no longer write, he asks the same questions and is given the same answers each time. In April 2014 he is hospitalised for lung and urinary infections, comes home to the house in Pedregal for palliative care, and dies at eight minutes past noon with Mercedes, Rodrigo, Gonzalo and the grandchildren in the rooms around him. He is eighty-seven. Mercedes, who has run the house for fifty-six years, survives him by six.
stops.quote: A person doesn't die when he should but when he can.
stops.quote_source: One Hundred Years of Solitude (1967), trans. Gregory Rabassa
suggested_refs: El País, coverage of 17 to 21 April 2014, for the official cause of death
sources: El País, April 2014 reporting (page blocked on refetch)

stops.name: Mexico City, the urn at Bellas Artes
stops.date_confidence: attested for the homage of 21 April 2014. The urn was present at the ceremony, which is not the same as a burial: the ashes were interred at Cartagena two years later, and accounts that make Bellas Artes the resting place are wrong.
stops.campa: Mexico holds the state homage in the Palacio de Bellas Artes, in the building where he was knocked to the floor thirty-eight years earlier. The presidents of Mexico and Colombia stand on the same platform and each of them claims him for his own country; he lived half his life in one and wrote all his books about the other. The queue of people carrying yellow flowers runs out of the doors and around the block. Yellow butterflies are released into the hall. The urn stays a few hours and then goes back to the family.
suggested_refs: The state homage at the Palacio de Bellas Artes, Mexico City, 21 April 2014

stops.name: Austin, the papers sold north
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Harry Ransom Center acquired the archive in 2014 and later published some 27,500 items online. The often-quoted purchase price of 2.2 million dollars appears in press coverage but not on the Center's own pages and is not asserted here. The month orders the segment.
stops.campa: The family sells the archive to the Harry Ransom Center at Austin: manuscripts, more than two thousand letters, forty photograph albums, notebooks, the typewriters and the computers, including drafts of Cien años de soledad with the corrections still on them. Colombian commentators ask why the papers of the national writer are in Texas. The Center digitises some twenty-seven thousand items and puts them online. In Madrid the following February a box of his effects is sealed into the Caja de las Letras vault at the Instituto Cervantes.
suggested_refs: The Gabriel García Márquez papers, Harry Ransom Center, University of Texas at Austin
The Caja de las Letras vault, Instituto Cervantes, Madrid, deposit of February 2015
sources: Harry Ransom Center research guide and 2020 exhibition pages

stops.name: Cartagena, the ashes at the Claustro de la Merced
stops.date_confidence: attested to 22 May 2016 per Spanish Wikipedia. The coordinate is the Claustro de la Merced of the Universidad de Cartagena and supersedes a slightly different value used elsewhere in the working material for the same site.
stops.campa: A portion of the ashes is set in the cloister of La Merced at the Universidad de Cartagena, inside the walls, a few streets from the newsroom of El Universal where a sub-editor once struck the adjectives out of his copy. He first came to this city at twenty-one, because the capital had burned and there was nowhere else to go, and registered here for a law degree he never took. A bronze bust by a Colombian sculptor stands over the urn. The university keeps the cloister open to anyone who walks in off the street.
suggested_refs: The Claustro de la Merced, Universidad de Cartagena, and the bust set over the urn in May 2016

stops.name: Mexico City, the book he ordered destroyed
stops.date_confidence: attested; En agosto nos vemos was published on 6 March 2024, what would have been his ninety-seventh birthday, against his instruction that the manuscript be destroyed. His sons have described the decision publicly as a betrayal.
stops.campa: Rodrigo and Gonzalo publish En agosto nos vemos, assembled from the drafts their father left behind when the memory failed, on what would have been his ninety-seventh birthday. He had told them the book did not work and was to be destroyed. They write in the preface that they are committing an act of betrayal and that the readers will decide whether it was worth it. The novel is short: a woman crosses to an island every August to put flowers on her mother's grave, and takes a different lover each time.
suggested_refs: En agosto nos vemos (2024) and the sons' preface
